title: Agent Desk
subtitle: Making two opposing metrics win at once — speed and compliance — in a high-stakes fintech verification workflow

indexedSections.title: Human middleware, at 3.2 days per application

value: ==Agent Desk is Best Egg's internal platform where verification agents approve or reject credit applications — personal loans, credit cards, and secured auto loans== — while staying inside fraud-prevention and compliance rules. Decisions here are irreversible, and they land on real people's credit outcomes.

The legacy system was fragmented and inconsistent across agent roles, forcing agents to act as "human middleware" — a 3.2-day bottleneck per application. As the solo designer, I owned the effort end-to-end: streamlining the workflow, defining measurable UX success metrics, and shipping inside a heavily regulated environment.

items.label: Constraint 1
items.title: Speed vs. compliance
items.desc: Workflows had to move faster without compromising fraud prevention, regulatory requirements, or auditability.

items.label: Constraint 2
items.title: Multiple agent roles
items.desc: Different agent types needed different levels of access, context, and decision authority inside the same workflow.

items.label: Constraint 3
items.title: Irreversible decisions
items.desc: Agents made frequent, irreversible calls under time pressure — fatigue and error risk compounded each other.

indexedSections.title: Two metrics that fight each other

items.label: Business wanted speed
items.desc: A single application took 3.2 days — a massive bottleneck.

items.label: Risk wanted rigor
items.desc: Verification rate sat at ~80% — too many valid applications weren't clearing.

value: The trap: these metrics are naturally opposed. Push agents to go faster and they get sloppy — verification rate drops. Tell them to slow down and scrutinize — time climbs. Most teams pick one.

blocks.label: The harder brief
blocks.value: Can both opposing metrics improve at the same time? That constraint ruled out brute force — more people, more time — and forced the solution to come from design decisions themselves.

indexedSections.title: Five decisions that broke the tradeoff

blocks.title: ==Find the real bottleneck (it wasn't a screen)==

value: With no dedicated researcher and a lean team, I used the lowest-cost, highest-signal method: live agent shadowing. Sitting beside agents on real cases, I watched them bounce across five or six systems — the legacy Agent Desktop, the internal Admin console, LoanPro, LexisNexis, raw spreadsheets — manually cross-checking the same data, leaning on tribal knowledge with no single source of truth.

blocks.label: The legacy reality — one verification, five systems

blocks.value: Opening Tab 1 for Admin, Tab 2 for LoanPro, Tab 3 for LexisNexis. I lose context every time I switch screens.
I have to scroll through 500+ items. I usually 'cherry-pick' the easy ones because I don't want a complex case right before lunch.

value: I mapped the end-to-end journey across five stages — Triage, Review & Verification, Investigation, Decision & Documentation, Outcome — and the emotional low points lined up exactly with the system gaps: overwhelmed at review, distracted mid-investigation, anxious at close-out, unsure whether anything was missed in the scattered data.

blocks.label: Five-stage journey map — emotion curve, verbatim quotes, and the design response per stage
The insight
blocks.value: The 3.2 days weren't lost inside any one screen — they were lost in the gaps between systems. Agents were literally human middleware, shuttling and reconciling data by hand.

value: So my first decision wasn't "make a page prettier." It was eliminate the middleware — consolidate scattered tools and data into one unified workspace: centralized application management across loan and credit card products, plus a Manager's Menu giving comprehensive access to customer data so agents stop reaching for external tools.

items.title: Centralized Application Management
items.desc: Manage loan and credit card applications in one unified workspace, with proactive alerts for potential data issues.

items.title: Manager's Menu
items.desc: Comprehensive access to customer data, reducing the need for external tools.

value: Here I hit a hard constraint. Agent cognitive load was brutal — but I couldn't cut information to reduce it. Compliance requires that every data point needed for verification stays visible; removing any of it risks the audit trail.
So the decision became: reduce load through structure, not subtraction.

items.title: Left–right split
items.desc: Mapped to the agent's mental model: customer data (to read) on the left, actions and CTAs (to do) on the right — making the "read, then decide" path legible in space.

items.title: Real-time Verification Checklist
items.desc: Previously tribal rules made explicit — every step consolidated, aligned with business rules, auto-resolving each item to "Clear" as it completes. Pending items stay surfaced at a glance.

items.title: Notes & History, always in view
items.desc: Persistent note entry and instant access to previous records, so context never has to be re-fetched from another system.

items.title: Clear CTAs
items.desc: Critical actions placed consistently and predictably at the end of the workflow — where the decision actually happens.

items.title: Verification Checklist
items.desc: All verification steps consolidated and aligned with business rules. Items update in real time and auto-resolve to "Clear" when complete.

items.title: Notes & History
items.desc: Always-visible note entry and access to previous records support informed decision-making.

value: Same information, zero removed — but the structure now carried the attention, serving both speed and accuracy at once. And because the layout is structural rather than role-specific, the same spatial logic held across agent roles with different access and decision authority — one mental model, many permission levels.

blocks.title: ==Design the right friction for irreversible actions==

value: Every agent click is irreversible — an approval or rejection that decides a real person's credit outcome and carries compliance weight.
Auto-resolving checklist items felt great, but over-automation risks automation complacency — agents blindly trusting the system. So I drew a line:

blocks.label: The line
blocks.value: Objective, checkable items auto-clear. Anything requiring human judgment must be confirmed by the agent.

value: I also added a Preview/Edit mode — a final review of changes before submission. On the surface this adds a step and fights the speed goal. My argument: in irreversible decisions, the rework and errors a preview prevents are worth far more than the two seconds it costs — slowing this one step makes the whole flow faster.
That's designing friction in the right place, inside compliance red lines that forbid one-click batch actions or skipped steps.

blocks.label: Preview/Edit mode — final review of changes before submission

blocks.value: Preview/Edit only works if the agent actually reads it — nothing forces genuine attention, only presence. It lowers the error rate; it doesn't guarantee it to zero.

value: The unified workspace surfaces proactive alerts for potential data issues — SSN mismatches, fraud flags, duplicate applications — before agents have to hunt for them. But I designed against an obvious second-order effect: too many alerts become alert fatigue. Agents go numb and ignore them, which is more dangerous than no alerts at all.
So alerts are tiered: only high-priority anomalies that genuinely affect the verification decision interrupt the agent; lower-priority ones degrade to quiet, passive hints.

blocks.value: Helping is only helping if it doesn't manufacture new noise.

blocks.label: Tiered alerts — high-priority interrupts vs. quiet inline hints

blocks.value: The tier boundary is a judgment call, not a formula — set it too loose and noise creeps back in; too strict and a real signal gets silently downgraded.

blocks.title: ==Define the metrics before designing, then prove it==

value: The most senior part of the work: I didn't design on gut. Before building, I partnered with the PM to define measurable UX success metrics up front — verification time, verification rate, and agent confidence — because without pre-defined metrics, you can't prove whether a decision was right.

Then I validated with shadowing plus rapid prototypes. I built competing layout directions — a Classic single-column layout (better readability, but dense and hard to scan) versus a Segmented tabbed layout (clear workflow stages, but hides data and adds clicks) — and tested them directly with agents, iterating on real feedback rather than my assumptions. The final left–right structure took the scannability of one and the workflow clarity of the other.

blocks.label: Layout explorations — Classic vs. Segmented, with agent-tested tradeoffs

value: The MVP launch received strong feedback from agents and leadership, with higher agent confidence and satisfaction reported.

Crucially, the two opposing metrics improved together — with distinct causal drivers: the unified workspace and explicit checklist removed cross-system shuttling (driving speed), while Preview/Edit and tiered alerts reduced misjudgment (driving verification rate).

blocks.value: Agent Desk 3.0 represents a major leap forward in our verification process — transforming how agents work and unlocking better customer experiences through cross-functional collaboration.

indexedSections.title: Put friction in the right place

value: The work I'm proudest of wasn't making a screen look good — it was finding, inside a pile of conflicting constraints (speed vs. compliance, lower load vs. can't-hide-data, automation vs. can't-blindly-trust), the one structure where everyone wins at once.

blocks.value: Frictionless finance was never about deleting friction — it's about putting friction in the right place.
